overview: Nurse midwives are advanced practice nurses who care for people through pregnancy, birth and the weeks after. They give prenatal checkups, monitor the baby's heartbeat and growth, deliver babies and provide gynecological care. O*NET rates knowledge of medicine at 4.82 out of 5 for this job and psychology at 4.33. Becoming one takes a nursing license plus a graduate degree in midwifery; 81% hold a master's degree in O*NET data. The BLS May 2025 median is $134,040, but there are only 7,920 jobs. Births are unpredictable, so long and irregular hours are common.
pay: Nurse midwives earn a median of $134,040, and the top 10% earn $188,320 or more. California stands far ahead with a state median of $203,840, 52% above the national figure, and it also has the most jobs, 870. Hawaii and Massachusetts follow, while North Dakota's median is $72,630.

faq.q: How much do nurse midwives make?
faq.a: The BLS May 2025 median is $134,040 a year. The middle half earn between $116,510 and $157,400. California ($203,840), Hawaii ($170,110) and Massachusetts ($159,800) pay the most. Pay is lowest in North Dakota, where the state median is $72,630.

faq.q: What degree do you need to be a nurse midwife?
faq.a: You need a registered nurse license and a graduate degree in nurse midwifery. In O*NET data, 81% of nurse midwives hold a master's degree and 16% a post-master's certificate. After school, you pass a national certification exam to become a Certified Nurse-Midwife (CNM).

faq.q: Is being a nurse midwife stressful?
faq.a: It can be. In O*NET data the job ranks above 94% of U.S. jobs for working more than 40 hours, and mistakes can have serious consequences. On-call nights are common. Many nurse midwives value the freedom to make decisions, which ranks above 90% of jobs.

faq.q: What jobs are similar to nurse midwife?
faq.a: The closest are postsecondary health specialties teachers (72% match), Midwives (72%) and Genetic Counselors (72%), based on O*NET 31.0. Health specialties teachers earn $107,310, 20% less than nurse midwives, according to BLS May 2025, and many work at nursing schools.
